hook.text: Every product team keeps a chart like this one. Each row is the users who first showed up in one month.

plan.text: The page asks fifteen questions. Six get a real query here. The other nine come quickly at the end, since the data analyst videos take them apart in depth.

join-in.text: The first piece: who came back at all.

join.text: Question one. Inner join or left join: which does a retention query need? Here are January's six active users, and February's four.

join-inner.text: An inner join keeps only the users found in both months: three rows. Count February's matches over those rows, and retention comes out at a hundred percent. The users who left were dropped before anything was counted.

join-left.text: A left join keeps all six January users and writes null where February has no match. Three out of six came back: fifty percent.

churn.text: Question two. How do you find users active one month but not the next? Those nulls are the answer. Keep the left join, and filter where February's user ID is null: users one, four and six. Not exists returns the same three.

rate-in.text: Retention is a rate, and every rate has a denominator that can be zero.

rate.text: Question three. How do you compute a rate without dividing by zero? Four variants in the page's funnel had no sessions at all. In Postgres, dividing by that zero is an error, and the whole query fails.

rate-nullif.text: Wrap the denominator in null if. It turns a zero into a null, so variant C gets a null rate: an honest blank. DuckDB returns null there anyway, but the habit keeps the query safe on every engine. And don't patch it with coalesce to zero. No sessions means no rate, not a rate of zero.

rate-int.text: Then watch integer division. In Postgres, a hundred twenty conversions over a thousand sessions is zero. Multiply by one point oh first, and it's point one two.

cohort-in.text: Now, the chart from the start.

cohort.text: Question four. How do you write a cohort retention query? Here's an activity log, made up for this video. Take each user's earliest month: that's their cohort. Then label every event with the months since that cohort.

cohort-count.text: Count distinct users by cohort and month offset. January's cohort starts with eight users, then six, four, and three.

cohort-rate.text: Divide each count by the cohort's month zero, and the counts become shares: a hundred, seventy-five, fifty, thirty-eight percent.

session-in.text: Months are coarse. Product teams also measure the smallest unit of use: one visit.

session.text: Question five. What is sessionization, and how do you do it in SQL? It groups one user's events into visits. A new session starts when the gap since their last event passes thirty minutes. User one has six hits in a day.

session-lag.text: Lag brings each row the timestamp before it. Flag a one where that gap is over thirty minutes, or where there's no earlier hit at all.

session-sum.text: Then a running sum of the flags is the session number. Gaps of ninety-five and two hundred five minutes start new sessions, so user one's six hits make three. Across all five users, twenty-four hits make twelve sessions.

pct-in.text: One more before the quick round: what counts as typical.

pct.text: Question six. How do you compute a median or a percentile in SQL? Here are twelve request times, made up for this video. Their average is four hundred seven milliseconds, slower than ten of the twelve requests.

pct-median.text: Percentile cont interpolates: the median is one sixty-five, halfway between the sixth and seventh values. Percentile disc returns a value that really occurred: one fifty.

pct-tail.text: That's why latency is reported as a percentile. The ninetieth percentile is eight hundred thirty-six milliseconds: nine requests in ten finish within it, and the slow tail stays in view instead of being averaged away.

rapid-in.text: The remaining nine are everyday patterns. Here they are, back to back.

r-having.text: Where filters rows before grouping, and having filters groups after. Put count in where, and DuckDB refuses: the aggregate doesn't exist yet.

r-window.text: Group by turns twenty-four sales into four region totals. A window function keeps all twenty-four rows and writes the total beside each one.

r-rank.text: On a tie, row number still counts one, two, three, four. Rank shares and then skips: one, two, two, four. Dense rank shares without the gap.

r-dod.text: For a day-over-day change, lag puts yesterday's amount on today's row, and you subtract. No self join needed.

r-topn.text: For the top N per group, number the rows inside each region by amount, then keep row numbers two or lower in an outer query.

r-running.text: A running total is an ordered sum: one hundred, three fifty, four twenty-five, six oh five. With no frame written, each sum covers the first row through this one, and rows tied on the day share one total.

r-latest.text: To keep the latest row per key, order each customer's orders newest first and keep row one: twelve customers, twelve rows.

r-pivot.text: Pivoting is conditional aggregation: a sum over case when the device is mobile, another for desktop, grouped by region.

r-count.text: And count star counts rows, count of a column skips its nulls, and count distinct counts unique values: eight views, six signed in, four people. That's volume against reach.

next.text: Every query here measured what users did. The newest round asks you to measure what a large language model, an LLM, writes. Next: LLM evaluation.

hook-cells.text: Each cell is the share of them still active a month later, then two, then three, so every row fades as it goes right. And each newer row is shorter: it has had fewer months to measure.

hook-sql.text: Building it is a classic data science SQL question, and each of its pieces gets asked on its own.

cohort-stair.text: Shares fall along each row, and the newest cohorts are the shortest: they've had the fewest months.
